newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Belgium on track for EMU, says PM Dehaene.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Belgium on track for EMU, says PM Dehaene.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said on Tuesday revisions to the 1997 budget agreed last weekend guaranteed Belgium a place in a single European currency from the start.

"The 1997 budget is of vital importance for our country because it will be part of our entry exam to (European economic and monetary union), which will be taken at the start of 1998," Dehaene said in a speech to parliament to present the outcome of the budget review.

"These revisions to the 1997 budget have made it possible to limit the budget deficit of all public authorities to 2.9 percent (of gross domestic product) which will allow our country to take part in EMU from the start," Dehaene added.
Dehaene said the new austerity measures represented only 1.1 percent of GDP, much less than has been required in neighbouring countries to keep on track for EMU.
"It is a certainty that Belgium is able to meet the convergence requirements of the Maastricht Treaty because the budget rests on a triple safety margin," Dehaene added.

First, Dehaene said, the deficit target at 2.9 percent was below the 3 percent norm permitted in the Maastricht Treaty. Secondly, the 1997 growth forecast was unchanged at 2.1 percent, compared with an average 2.9 percent of recent forecasts. Thirdly, there is a 20 billion franc safety margin designed to counter possible adverse developments on financial markets.
Belgium was also on course to cut its debt to 127 percent of GDP in 1997, which is 10 percentage points less than in 1993.
Dehaene added the fight against unemployment would be the focus of the second half of the government's four-year term in office, which began in May 1995.
Dehaene said that before its summer recess, the government would organise five special cabinet meetings, each focusing on single issue problems.

The five issues were: job creation and small and medium-sized companies; information and telecommunication technologies; the functioning of the civil service; improving democracy on the basis of recommendations of an all-party parliamentary working group; and the fight against poverty and social exclusion.
